narrative:
The model determined that you have a 99.2% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to decide who is likely to succeed in law school and beyond, your application was rejected.

The strongest reason for this outcome was your class ranking at the end of your third year, which placed you far below the typical student who is admitted. This single factor pushed the prediction heavily toward failure. Your first-year ranking was the second most important influence and also moved the outcome in the same negative direction, showing that your academic performance in the early and later stages of college both raised serious concerns. Family income was the third most influential piece of information; being in the upper-middle bracket slightly increased the predicted risk compared with the mix of incomes among accepted students.

Taken together, these three factors created a clear picture for the model that your academic record did not match the profile of students who reliably pass the bar. Gender and race played no role in the decision.

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses or pursue a graduate program, aim for a significantly higher LSAT score, and consider targeted bar-preparation resources before reapplying. Demonstrating consistent improvement in rigorous coursework will be the most powerful way to change future predictions. (218 words)
